readingInstruction: Read Ezekiel 29:1-32:32. This is a survey day. These chapters are oracles against Egypt and its Pharaoh, including the famous images of the crocodile in the Nile and the great tree cut down. Read for the theme: pride before God is brought low.
settingTheScene: Ezekiel’s seven oracles against Egypt fill these chapters. Judah had often looked to Egypt for help against Babylon, and Egypt had often failed her. The oracles say that God will humble Egypt, and that she will never again be a source of false security for Israel. They are dated to the siege of Jerusalem and afterward, between 587 and 571 BC.
observation: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, My Nile is my own; I made it for myself” (29:3).
“You have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel” (29:6).
“And it shall be the most lowly of the kingdoms, and never again exalt itself above the nations” (29:15).
“And they will know that I am the LORD” (29:21, one of many repetitions).
“Whom are you like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon” (31:2-3).
“Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because it towered high… I will give it into the hand of a mighty one among the nations” (31:10-11).
“They lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword” (32:32).
interpretation:
Egypt is addressed as a great crocodile in the Nile who claims, “My Nile is my own; I made it for myself.” It is a claim of self-creation, the essence of pride. God will pull him out with hooks in his jaws and leave him in the desert. Egypt had been a “staff of reed” to Israel. When Judah leaned on it, it splintered and pierced their hand. The lesson is that trusting in political alliances rather than in God is a broken support.

The oracles describe Egypt’s fall in various images: a land laid waste, a sword coming on Cush and Put, a Pharaoh with a broken arm. God will scatter the Egyptians and bring them back after forty years, but as a lowly kingdom that never again rules. The reason is not only for judgment, but “then they will know that I am the LORD.”

Chapter 31 compares Pharaoh to the great cedar of Lebanon, a tree that towered above all others in the garden of God. All the birds nested in its boughs. But it was proud, and God cut it down. The lesson is for Egypt by comparing it to Assyria, which had been another great tree and was cut down. If Assyria fell, so will Egypt.

Chapter 32 contains two laments over Pharaoh and a picture of his descent to Sheol, among the uncircumcised and the slain, in the company of Assyria, Elam, and others. The nations are brought down to the pit, one after another. It is a solemn picture of the equality of death. All who exalt themselves will lie among the dead.

The main message in all of these oracles is simple: God rules over the nations. No power, however great, is beyond his hand. It is a comfort for those who feel crushed by empires, and a warning for those who think they are secure.
connection: Acts 12:21-23 shows Herod struck down for accepting worship as a god. Isaiah 31:1 warns against going down to Egypt for help. Luke 1:52: “He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate.” Psalm 20:7: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.” Matthew 2:13-15 shows God calling his Son out of Egypt.
application:
Think of a “staff of reed” you have leaned on: a person, a plan, or a resource that has broken. Place your weight on God instead.

Pray for nations experiencing the pride of power and for those who suffer under it.

Remember that God rules history, and that no power is permanent.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as ruler over every nation.
Ask him to forgive where you lean on reed staffs.
Tell him whom you trust, and give it to him.
